application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The analysis of systems executing a set of transactions composed by a number of tasks is required in some application domains, such as distributed systems or many audio/ video streaming systems. This paper deals with the time response analysis of such systems, considering periodic uniprocessor transactions, and tasks, characterized by their fixed priority and execution time, connected in series through bounded buffers. The scheduling policy allows several transaction jobs to be active at a time, which is possible by putting intermediate task results in the buffers. When the output buffer of a task is full, the task becomes blocked and priority inversion arises. An analysis method is described that allows to calculate the worst-case response time of the transactions in order to be compared with their end-to-end deadlines. Besides, the results of the method application show how task priorities or buffer sizes influence the transaction response times.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: RMA (Rate Monotonic Analysis) [1] allows the calculation of the response time of tasks in a wide range of uniprocessor real-time systems, based on fixed-priority scheduling. Widely accepted techniques [2] [3] have been proposed for the analysis of real-time systems composed by tasks with precedence relations. These works pose no assumptions on the size of the intermediate buffers used to communicate consecutive tasks in the transactions. However, in some types of applications it is required to bound the maximum size of these buffers, either due to the limited amount of available memory or to the size of the messages. This situation is typical in multimedia applications, specially for audio and video processing, which are usually implemented as a kind of streaming transactions that can be seen as chains composed by an input task, an output task and a number of filter tasks executing a specific algorithm to improve the quality of the data. This scheme is followed by the TSSA architecture (TriMedia Streaming Software Architecture) [4], which is a template used to develop multimedia applications for the TriMedia processor system [5].

In the case of high volume electronics, designers try to minimize the size of intermediate buffers due to cost constrains. This implies that the size cannot be modelled to be unlimited when trying to analyse such kind of systems. On the other hand, consumer devices (e.g. TV sets) must ensure high output quality, which in some cases may imply that a task could be occasionally blocked because its output buffer is full, in order to avoid data losses. This is a case of priority inversion which had not been considered by the available response time analysis techniques. In addition, a proper assignment of priorities to tasks within a transaction could help to enforce desired behaviours. A response time analysis technique will assist designers to find an assignment of priorities to tasks and sizes to buffers, in such a way that end-to-end deadlines are met, the buffer memory is minimised, and no input data are missed. The current lack of suitable analysis techniques implies that such assignments are often made by trial-and-error, which increases the development time of applications.

In [6] a framework has been stated to consider different fixed priority levels among tasks within each transaction in uniprocessor systems, but no intermediate buffers are considered. Other works in which intermediate buffers are used to communicate tasks are [7] and [8]. In the first one, streaming chains are analysed by assuming that their tasks form a V-shaped fixed priority distribution and that intermediate buffers can never be overflowed. In the second one, chains are analysed by considering an EDF scheduling algorithm with, again, no overflowed buffers.

In this paper, an extension of the main premises stated in [9] is done in order to describe a technique to analyse the end-to-end response time of transactions composed by a number of tasks connected in series and communicated through bounded buffers, which could be occasionally overflowed. Some preliminary results and conclusions of its application are also included. The analysis technique poses now a number of restrictions to the type of transactions to be analysed, which may limit its utility. However, it is the base work for analysis techniques under development where these restrictions will be gradually removed.

div.head: System model
div.p: The model considered in our work is based on that used in [6], but with some additional parameters and restrictions derived from the particular characteristics of the kind of system we are interested in. Thus, we model a streaming system as consisting of a set of n concurrent transactions (τ i , for i=1,..., n) that perform some periodical (T i ) processing by executing m(i) sequential tasks (τ ij ) from an input to an output. Each transaction has a chain or sequential topology, in the sense that each pair of consecutive tasks τ ij and τ ij+1 are connected through a bounded buffer, i.e. a FIFO queue q ij with a length of N ij positions (see Figure 1). On the other hand, each task τ ij is characterized by its computation time (C ij ) and its priority (P ij ). Initially, it is considered that transactions have their own priority ranges, which do not overlap. It is assumed that τ 1 is the lowest priority transaction and τ n is the highest priority one.

Therefore, a transaction job τ i (k) is started each time some data (element or token number k, which could be considered to be something from a video frame to an audio sample) is put (by an external device) into the input queue (q i0 ) in order to be processed by the transaction. In turn, each time a task is executed, it processes data (removes a token) from its input queue and stores data (puts a token) in its output queue during C ij . Therefore, τ ij is not ready to execute until there is at least one element in q ij-1 and one available position in q ij . We are also considering a preemptive fixed priority scheduler that dispatches first the task with the oldest pending token, when there are two or more active jobs ready to execute in equal priority tasks. Furthermore, transactions do not suspend themselves at any time between their activation and their completion, overhead time related to task scheduling is ignored and queues are supposed to be initially empty.

div.head: Problem description
div.p: The first question to deal with is whether transaction jobs are processed in time, for those applications in which an end-to-end transaction deadline (D i ) exists. The proposed method to achieve this goal consists of calculating the worst-case transaction response time in order to be compared with D i [6] [10]. From the model presented above, it is possible that a transaction has several active jobs at the same time, which should only be accepted when D i >T i . Consequently, several tokens can be stored in the transaction queues and even some queues could be overflowed. When deadlines are greater than periods, it is not sufficient to analyse the first job of a transaction. As shown in [10], it is necessary to extend the analysis to a busy period, that for a given transaction τ i , is the maximum time interval within which the processor executes transactions at priority level higher than or equal to the lowest priority of any task belonging to τ i . In this case, the length (L i ) of this busy period can be calculated with (EQ 1), which is based on [6] and which will be finite when the processor load is less than 100%. The term C p stands for the whole computation time of a transaction τ p . (EQ 2) allows us to calculate NJ i , which is the number of jobs included in a τ i -busy period started at a critical instant.

div.p: A transaction meets its deadline if (EQ 3) is satisfied for all jobs within a τ i -busy period. CT(τ i (k)) and R(τ i (k)) are the worst-case completion time and response time, respectively, of the k th job of τ i . Note that D i should be limited to an upper bound max(D i ) in such a way that the number of tokens activated in τ i during that time does not exceed the storage capacity of the transaction because, otherwise, some input data could be lost.

The novel problem addressed in this paper is motivated by the consideration of bounded buffers. As in [3] or [6], the k th job of τ ij (τ ij (k)) must be executed after τ ij-1 (k). But now, a second precedence relation appears: τ ij (k) must also be executed after τ ij+1 (k-N ij ), as illustrated in Figure 2.

In such a scenario, a transaction job may suffer not only from external interference (EI) due to the execution of higher priority transactions, as in [6], but also from selfinterference due to other active jobs executing in higher priority tasks within the same transaction (SI). In turn, SI consists of two components, a forward self-interference

div.head: Previous simplifications and remarks
div.p: In order to simplify the analysis, two reduced forms of a transaction are used. Thus, the calculation of the completion time of each transaction job is based on the canonical form of the transaction, defined in [6]. As a summary, the canonical form of τ i can be seen as a new transaction τ' i composed of m'(i) sequential tasks (τ' ij ), with , characterized each by its computation time (C' ij ) and its priority (P' ij ). The priorities of τ' i do not decrease from input to output. An example of τ i and τ' i is shown in Figure 4. Since the precedence relation between task jobs considered in [6] is still valid here, the calculation of CT(τ i (k)) can be also based now on the consecutive analysis of the canonical tasks, i.e. CT(τ' ij (k)) is based on CT(τ' ij-1 (k)). On the other hand, since CT(τ' ij (k)) is calculated to be equal to the completion time of the last task included in τ' ij , (EQ 4) is true.

As a novel contribution of this work, a new form of a transaction, called reverse-canonical (RC) form, is introduced. For τ i it is defined as a new transaction τ'' i composed of m''(i) sequential tasks (τ'' ij ), with , characterized each by its computation time (C'' ij ) and its priority (P'' ij ). The priorities of τ'' i do not increase from input to output. Figure 3 includes the algorithm to obtain the RC form of a transaction τ i , and Figure 4 shows an example of the priority distribution of τ i and τ'' i . In any case, (EQ 5) is always met.

The RC form is useful to analyse the way in which tokens move through a transaction. Thus, the priority pro-files shown in Figure 4 help to understand that, while there are no overflowed queues, a token can only enter a RC task if the previous ones have reached its output queue and there are no newer tokens executing in previous RC tasks. For this reason, queues separating consecutive RC tasks are the first to be overflowed. Also it can be seen that BSI over τ' ij (k) is the computation time of those RC tasks with P>P' ij multiplied by the number of jobs activated during the response time of τ' ij (k). Once one of these queues is overflowed, other previous queues within the same RC task may become also full, which implies that tokens cannot reach its output and, then, BSI cannot longer be calculated in that way. What is clear is that the accounting of the number of tokens within τ i and the queues they can be in is a critical point for the response time analysis.

Another interesting remark that can be better understood by observing the priority levels of Figure 4, is that FSI can only affect τ' i1 (k), for . This is because, by definition, the first job of a τ i -busy period can never be affected by other previous one and because, due to priority reasons, a token can only leave τ' i1 once the previous one has left the transaction, which is also true in [6]. It is important to recall that we are calculating the response time for the whole transaction, based on the canonical form. We are not dealing with the particular completion time for intermediate tasks within canonical segments.

div.head: Case studies and results
div.p: The previously described analysis technique has been implemented for validation and experimentation purposes. In this section, the results of the analysis of some case studies are shown, in order to illustrate the type of results and conclusions that the method allows to achieve. In particular, it is analysed the response time of a transaction for different sizes of its buffers and priority assignments.

Those cases are based on the kind of streaming systems that can be implemented with the TSSA architecture [4]. In our example we have three applications processing concurrently incoming audio and/or video flows into the CPU. Application data are given in Table 1, being the lowest priority (τ 1 ) the one to be analysed. From the two interfering transactions, one (τ 3 ) has a low frequency but a long computation time and the other (τ 2 ) has a high frequency but a short computation time, being the total processor load equal to 66%.

Besides, let us suppose that τ 1 is composed of 15 simple tasks, each executing a certain type of data processing, with the computation times shown in Table 2. Although this number of tasks may be too big for a common transaction, it has allowed us to test the analysis technique in a complex situation. The analysis performed is based on varying the queue lengths and task priorities, in order to know how these changes affect the transaction behaviour. Now some combinations between queue lengths and priorities can be analysed.

• Increasing priority case. If the task priorities are assigned in an increasing way, the transaction is in its canonical form and it is a single RC task. Since P 11 is the lowest, there can be at most one token being processed by the transaction, no matter the queue lengths. In such a case, although the response time for the transaction is the shortest, this priority distribution is not always appropriate: when using the same buffer size setting, it is easier to lose input data with this priority distribution than with the others. • Decreasing priority case. If the task priorities are assigned in a decreasing way, the transaction is in its RC form and it is a single canonical task. Since P 11 is the highest, each time a new token is put in q 10 it can enter the transaction and its response time depends decisively on the queue lengths.

This task should be substituted by all the tasks that are between the first and the last task whose priorities are equal to the lowest within the transaction, if there were more than one. • Application-specific or random priority case. If we consider a more general case then different tasks, canonical tasks and RC tasks can be identified. Figure 6 shows how the maximum response time of the transaction, i.e. max(R(τ 1 (k))), varies when all the queue lengths are increased from 1 to a certain value, for the three cases proposed above. Note that, since q 10 is placed before the first task, it does not influence the time response but it may avoid input data loses. For this study, N 10 is considered to be 1. It can be seen in Figure 6 that, as expected, the minimum of max(R(τ 1 (k))) is achieved for the case of increasing priorities, no matter the queue lengths, because jobs do not suffer from SI. However, in this case max(D 1 ) is very low, i.e. it is equal to 2T 1 =200 because only two active tokens are allowed, one in q 10 and other executing in τ 1 . Such priority distribution is clearly not acceptable because max(R(τ 1 (k)))>max(D 1 ). For the case of decreasing priorities, it can be seen in Figure 6 that max(R(τ 1 (k))) is maximum and increases as queue lengths increase until a maximum value. Nevertheless, max(D 1 ) increases faster than max(R(τ 1 (k))). This issue can be better understood by means of Figure 7A in which the maximum number of active tokens (MN i ), that can be calculated as in (EQ 17), is represented for each queue length. The the total queue capacity or memory requirement is also represented, which determines max(D 1 ). Those queue lengths for which the maximum number of active tokens is greater than the total queue capacity cannot be accepted (unitary lengths in Figure 7A). However, it is not necessary to increase all queue lengths in order to increase max(D 1 ). Thus, for example, if only the input queue of the last RC task is increased, while the rest of queues have unitary length, the total memory needs increase softer (see Figure 7B) and, moreover, max(R(τ 1 (k))) increases in a more linear and tractable way until the same maximum value (see Figure 8). This high-lights the special influence of the input queue of the last RC task in a transaction. As it can be deduced also from Figure 7, queue lengths do not need to be infinite to avoid overflows. For example, note that 37 is the maximum number of active tokens represented in Figure 7, so queues with a length greater than 37 will never be overflowed and, moreover, any queue length over 37 will not vary the transaction time response, (see Figure 6).

div.p: For the general application specific case, overflows are avoided even reducing queues inside RC tasks to a unitary length if queues between RC tasks have at least MN 1 positions, i.e. 27 positions in this case from (EQ 17). But, not only this, if all queues have unitary length except the input queue of the last RC task, that has at least MN 1 positions, then the worst-case time response is not affected. This fact can be deduced from the three curves of Figure 9, that represent max(R(τ 1 (k))) for the random priority case varying all queues; varying the input queues of RC tasks, keeping the rest as unitary; and varying only the input queue of the last RC task, also keeping the rest as unitary. It can be seen in that figure that, indeed, the three curves coincide for queues longer than 27. However, as it can be deduced, the

(EQ 17) total memory needs for that length is much less for the third curve because only one queue has such a length. For other shorter queues, overflows generate priority inversion and BSI is lower, which makes that the third curve is quite lower than the other two. Therefore, we can conclude that: • Changes on task priority distribution and buffer sizes have inverse effects over max(R(τ 1 (k))) and max(D 1 ).

• Transaction time response can be tuned by choosing suitable queue lengths under MN 1 , that is a bound over which the time response is not affected. • Queue length assignment should keep a reasonable balance between max(D 1 ) and memory requirements. In this sense, these variables can be managed in a quite linear way and kept within acceptable ranges by varying only the input queue of the last RC task.

div.head: Conclusions and future work
div.p: This paper presents a theoretical method to analyse the worst-case response time of periodic streaming transactions, consisting of a chain of tasks with different priorities and computation times connected through bounded buffers, which could be a suitable model for certain applications running in high-volume electronic consumer audio/video devices. The main goal of this technique is to help designers to reduce the development time of such applications. During the analysis, the response time of each transaction can be compared with its end-to-end deadline in order to know if it is met or not. Since there can be several active jobs of a transaction, the concepts of forward and backward self-interference are used and they are calculated based on the canonical and reverse-canonical forms of the transaction, by taking into account the possibility of buffer overflows.

The results extracted from different case studies illustrate how priority distribution among tasks in a transaction and how the length of its queues, until a definite upper bound, influence its time response. The method could then be used by system designers as a means of making early estimations about how task priorities or internal buffer sizes influence the application time behaviour, which may help them, in turn, to tune quickly such parameters in a suitable way.

We are working now on the response time analysis of the input task of each transaction, which will allow us to determine if some input data could be lost, as well as on other more general cases like any priority distribution among transactions, time-driven output, no periodic input, etc. It is also planned to experiment with other scheduling techniques, in order to know their merits for dealing with this type of applications.
